title: Common nested-if mistakes
idea: Wrong indentation sends a branch to the wrong if, and = vs == still bites. Spot the flaw and explain why it misbehaves.

options: The else lines up with the OUTER if, so it runs for under-18s, not for ticketless adults
exercises.explanation: Indentation decides ownership. This else matches the outer if, so it answers 'age >= 18', not the inner ticket question. Indent it to match the inner if instead.

exercises.prompt: What actually prints above when age = 15, has_ticket = True?
exercises.explanation: age >= 18 is False, so the outer else runs: 'Buy a ticket'. That is clearly wrong for a 15-year-old - proof the else is attached to the wrong if.

options: 'is_admin = True' uses one =, which assigns; a test needs == (or just 'if is_admin:')
exercises.explanation: A single = assigns and is not allowed in an if test. Use 'if is_admin == True:' or, better, 'if is_admin:'. The = vs == trap applies inside nested ifs too.

exercises.prompt: Indenting the inner if by a different amount than Python expects can cause an error or send it to the wrong block.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Indentation is meaningful in Python. Mismatched indent either errors out or quietly attaches the line to the wrong block.

options: The inner if is not indented, so Python can't see it is inside the outer if
exercises.explanation: The inner if must be indented under the outer if. With no indent, Python expects the outer if to have a body and raises an error.
With only the all-True case needed, 'and' is flatter and clearer. Nest only when an in-between case needs its own branch.

exercises.prompt: Why is a deeply over-nested if (if inside if inside if inside if) a smell to watch for?
options: It gets hard to read and trace; often 'and'/elif can flatten it
Python forbids more than two levels
It runs slower than the hardware
exercises.explanation: Deep nesting is legal but hard to follow. If the branches don't each need their own response, combine conditions with 'and' or use elif to flatten.
Use == to compare. A single = would try to assign to role and is not valid in an if condition.

exercises.prompt: A nested if has an inner if with no else. For the inner-False case, what happens?
options: Nothing is printed by the inner block; the program just continues
exercises.explanation: An if without an else simply does nothing when its condition is False. Don't expect the outer else to catch an inner-False case - it won't.

exercises.prompt: Best habit to avoid nested-if bugs?
options: Line up each else with the if it answers, and trace every path
Always nest at least three deep
exercises.explanation: Careful indentation decides which if an else belongs to, and tracing every path catches a branch attached to the wrong question.
